title: How to start selling on Amazon Canada in 2026: complete beginner's guide
description: Sell on Amazon.ca in 2026: CAD 29.99 plan, referral and FBA fees, GST/HST/PST/QST, bilingual labels, US tariffs and your first 90 days.
tldr: The Professional plan costs CAD 29.99 a month (Individual: CAD 1.49 per unit sold) and one North America Unified Account covers Amazon.ca, Amazon.com and Amazon.com.mx [s1][s2].
Most categories pay a 15% referral fee with a CAD 0.40 minimum; computers and consumer electronics pay 8% [s38].

FBA fulfilment starts at CAD 4.46 (envelope) or CAD 5.92 (standard, first 100 g), plus a 3.5% fuel surcharge since April 17, 2026 and holiday peak fees from Oct 15, 2026 to Jan 14, 2027 [s38][s4][s37].
Amazon collects GST/HST on your Amazon.ca sales until you register; you must register once sales pass CAD 30,000 in a quarter or four quarters [s10][s13].
Amazon collects PST/RST/QST in BC, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec on eligible sales shipped from inside Canada [s10].
Labels need English and French; Quebec's stricter Bill 96 (Law 14) rules on product packaging and trademarks took effect June 1, 2025 [s31][s33].
US–Canada tariffs changed again in 2026, including a US 10% tariff on non-CUSMA Canadian goods and new Canadian counter-tariffs; check CBSA and canada.ca for current rates [s20][s24].
Plan 90 days: listing, Vine, Sponsored Products, weekly search-term clean-up, then decide on a second product or Amazon.com.

blocks.p: Amazon.ca is Amazon's store for Canada. It is smaller than Amazon.com, but it is not a separate world. Since Amazon runs the US, Canadian and Mexican stores from one **North America Unified Account**, a seller who opens a Professional account can list in all three stores without paying a second subscription [s1][s2]. That one fact shapes everything else in this guide: many sellers on Amazon.ca are also US sellers, and many Canadian sellers also sell into the US.

Amazon does not publish a public count of Amazon.ca sellers or new sellers per year, and we could not find a trustworthy independent figure for 2026. Treat any blog number you see with care. What you can see for yourself is the competition on the search page for your product idea: how many listings, how many reviews the top sellers have, and how many sellers share the same listing.

blocks.h3: What makes Canada different from the US store

ul: **Two official languages.** Product labels must carry key information in English and French, and Quebec has its own stricter French-language law (Bill 96, also called Law 14) [s31][s33]. Many foreign sellers skip this. That is a risk for them and a gap for you.

**Provincial taxes.** Canada has a federal GST, some provinces fold it into one HST, and others add their own PST or QST. Amazon now collects most of these for you in most cases, but not all, and the rules change if you register [s10][s15].

**Tariffs with the US.** 2025 and 2026 brought a trade fight between Canada and the US, with tariffs and counter-tariffs that changed several times [s18][s20][s23]. If your stock crosses that border, this matters to your costs.

**Fewer sellers per listing in some niches.** Because Canada needs bilingual labels, separate tax handling and a separate inventory pool for FBA, some large US brands simply don't stock Amazon.ca well. Look for products where the top Amazon.ca listings are out of stock, shipped slowly from the US, or have English-only images and text.

blocks.p: Amazon's AI shopping assistant, Rufus, answers shopper questions using your listing text, images, Q&A and reviews. Check whether it shows in your Amazon.ca app and in which language; either way, write listings that answer the real questions a buyer asks (size, what's in the box, who it's for) in plain words. On the low-price side, Amazon.ca runs a **Low-Price FBA** rate: products priced under CAD 14 get FBA rates CAD 0.80 lower than standard [s38]. That makes very cheap items more competitive, so a beginner should avoid racing to the bottom on price.

callout.title: What this means for a beginner
callout.text: Amazon.ca is a good first store if you live in Canada or can handle bilingual labels and Canadian tax. Your edge is doing the boring Canadian things well: French on the pack, stock in Canadian warehouses, fast delivery and correct tax setup.

callout.title: Fee tables online are often US numbers
callout.text: Many 2026 fee guides are written for Amazon.com and quote USD rates. Amazon.ca fees are in CAD and are different. Always use the Amazon.ca Revenue Calculator and the fee pages in Seller Central Canada.

blocks.p: Amazon itself pitches Canada to US sellers as a natural next step, and its own 'selling in Canada' guide walks through the same unified account [s3]. Independent guides make the same point and add that Canadian tax and labelling are where most newcomers trip up [s35].

ul: You live in Canada, have a Canadian bank account and want to sell to people near you first.
You already sell on Amazon.com and want a second store with less crowding. With a Professional plan the extra store adds no second subscription [s1][s2].
Your product can carry English and French labels without a big redesign.
Your goods are made in Canada, or you can prove CUSMA origin, which helps if you later sell into the US [s24].
Your product is heavy or bulky. Shipping and FBA fees for large items eat thin margins.
Your product is a regulated category in Canada (children's products, cosmetics, natural health products, food) and you don't yet know the Health Canada rules.
Your only plan is to buy from US suppliers and resell in Canada. Counter-tariffs on some US goods changed several times in 2025–2026 [s18][s20].

blocks.h3: If you live outside Canada (India, China, the US and elsewhere)

ul: You can register through the North America Unified Account. If you register through the US store (a North America and Brazil unified account) you pay USD 39.99 a month; a Canada account used only for Canada costs CAD 29.99 a month [s2].
You will need a way to receive payouts. Amazon supports bank accounts in many countries; check the current list during registration.

Under Canada's platform rules, a non-resident seller who is not registered for GST/HST and does not carry on business in Canada generally does not have to register when selling goods through a platform like Amazon, because Amazon collects the tax [s11][s12]. Ask a Canadian tax adviser if you hold stock in Canada, since the rules depend on your facts.
Your labels still need a Canadian dealer name and address if the product is made outside Canada, under the Consumer Packaging and Labelling rules [s33][s34].

callout.title: Currency
callout.text: Amazon.ca prices and fees are in CAD. If your costs are in USD, INR or CNY, build your price on a conservative exchange rate so a swing doesn't wipe out your margin.

blocks.p: Most serious beginners should pick Professional. You need it to run Sponsored Products ads and to use many brand tools. If you sell fewer than about 20 units a month, Individual is cheaper (20 × CAD 1.49 = CAD 29.80), but you give up ads.

blocks.h3: What you need before you start

ul: A government-issued photo ID (passport or driver's licence) that matches your name exactly.
A bank account that can receive payouts, and a chargeable credit card.
A phone number and email you control for the long term.
Your business details if you register as a company: legal name, address and registration number. A Canadian business also has a nine-digit Business Number (BN) once it registers with the CRA [s13].
A recent bank or credit card statement showing the same name and address, since Amazon often asks for one.

ol: Go to Sell on Amazon Canada and start registration with a new email (not your shopping account if you can avoid it).
Choose Individual or Professional.
Enter business type, legal name and address exactly as on your documents.
Upload your ID and a statement. Amazon may also ask for a live video call or an in-person check. Join on time with the original documents.
Add your bank account and credit card.
Fill in the tax interview. Canadian sellers can add a GST/HST number here if they have one [s10][s17].
Wait for verification. Answer any request in Seller Central quickly and exactly.
Once approved, set up two-step verification and check that the US and Mexico stores are visible in the marketplace switcher [s2].

blocks.h3: Common reasons for delay or rejection

ul: Name or address on the statement does not match the ID or the form.
Blurry or cropped document photos, or expired ID.
Using a virtual office or mailbox address that Amazon cannot verify.
Linking to an earlier account that was suspended. Amazon treats related accounts as one.
Missing the video call slot.

callout.title: One account only
callout.text: Do not open a second seller account to 'start fresh'. Amazon links accounts by identity, payment and device, and a second account without permission can get both suspended.

blocks.p: Amazon.ca charges you in layers: a plan fee, a referral fee on every sale, and, if you use FBA, fulfilment and storage fees. Ads, samples, photos and stock are on top. blocks.h3: Storage, inbound and other FBA fees

ul: **Monthly storage** is charged per cubic metre of daily average volume: CAD 40 (standard size) and CAD 28 (oversize) from January to September, rising to CAD 77 and CAD 49 from October to December [s38].
**Aged inventory** surcharges apply to stock stored over about 180 days, and a high storage utilization fee can apply too [s38][s36]. Send small batches at first.
**Inbound placement service** fees apply to some standard and large bulky shipments [s36]; check the current rates in Seller Central Canada rather than US guides.
**Returns processing** (when Amazon offers the buyer free return shipping) and **removal/disposal** orders are charged per item [s36]. Check the current amounts in Seller Central.
**Refund administration fee**: when you refund a buyer, Amazon returns your referral fee minus the lesser of CAD 5.00 or 20% of that referral fee [s38].
**FBA New Selection** can give eligible new products free inbound shipping, storage, removals and returns processing, with conditions [s36].

blocks.p: Amazon's fees carry GST/HST. If you are registered for GST/HST you can usually claim this back as input tax credits; if you are not registered it is simply a cost [s17].

We did not find a credible, current public figure for average Amazon.ca cost per click. Use the suggested bid range the Amazon Ads console shows for your own keywords; it reflects your category today.

blocks.h3: Who collects: Amazon as marketplace facilitator

ul: Amazon says marketplace facilitator rules are in effect across Canada. It calculates, collects and remits tax on eligible third-party sales shipped from within Canada; imports from outside Canada are excluded [s10].
Provincial dates on Amazon's page: Saskatchewan PST from Jul 1, 2021; Quebec QST from Nov 1, 2021; Manitoba RST from Dec 1, 2021; British Columbia PST from Jul 1, 2022 [s10].

Federal GST/HST: Amazon collects it only when you are **not** registered for GST/HST. Once your GST/HST number is in Seller Central, Amazon stops collecting it and passes it to you in your payout, and you remit it to the CRA [s10][s17].
A simplified GST/HST registration (numbers ending in RT9999) is treated as unregistered for Amazon.ca sales [s16].
Under the federal rules from July 1, 2021, a registered platform operator must charge GST/HST on goods sold through it by unregistered vendors, resident or not [s11][s12].
**Canadian residents:** you must register for GST/HST once your taxable sales pass CAD 30,000 in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive quarters (the 'small supplier' test) [s13][s14].
You can register voluntarily below that, mainly to claim back GST/HST paid on Amazon fees and business costs as input tax credits [s14][s17].
Registration is online through the CRA's Business Registration Online. You get a nine-digit Business Number (BN) plus an RT0001 program account for GST/HST [s13].
**Quebec residents** deal with Revenu Québec for QST [s14].

**Non-residents** selling through Amazon who are not registered and don't carry on business in Canada generally don't need to register under the platform measure [s11]. The CRA's simplified regime is built for digital services and does not let you claim input tax credits [s12]. Get advice if you keep stock in Canadian warehouses.

blocks.p: Your Amazon profit is business income. A sole proprietor reports it on their personal return; a corporation files its own return. Keep every invoice, Amazon settlement report and shipping bill. Non-residents should also check their home-country rules and any tax treaty.

callout.title: When to hire an accountant
callout.text: Get a Canadian accountant who knows Amazon before you pass the small-supplier threshold, before you register for GST/HST, if you hold stock in Canada as a non-resident, or the first time you import goods. A one-hour setup call is cheaper than fixing a year of wrong filings.

blocks.p: Some categories need Amazon's approval before you can list, and some products are banned. Check 'Add a product' in Seller Central: if it says you need approval, read the requirements before you order stock. Common examples are grocery, health and personal care items, toys in Q4 and some branded products.

ul: Most consumer products fall under the **Canada Consumer Product Safety Act (CCPSA)**, run by Health Canada. It bans products that are a danger to health or safety and sets specific regulations for many product types.

**Children's products** (toys, cribs, car seats, anything for young kids) have strict rules on things like lead, small parts and flammability. Read Health Canada's guidance for your exact product before you buy.
If you learn of a serious safety incident with your product, the law requires you to report it to Health Canada within short deadlines. Read the current CCPSA incident-reporting guidance.
Cosmetics, natural health products, food and medical devices have their own separate Health Canada rules. Avoid these as a first product unless you know them well.
Under the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act and Regulations, prepackaged consumer products must show the **product identity** in both English and French [s33][s34].
The **net quantity** must be shown; metric symbols count as bilingual [s33].
For products made wholly outside Canada, the label must show the identity and principal place of business of the person in Canada responsible, or follow the rules for foreign dealers [s34].
Extra information such as directions and marketing text does not have to be bilingual federally, but Quebec is stricter [s33].

Quebec's Charter of the French Language requires French on product packaging, labels, inserts, instructions and warranties. Another language can appear, but generally not more prominently than the French [s31][s32].

From Jun 1, 2025, generic or descriptive words on packaging need French even when they are part of a trademark. A trademark can generally stay only in another language if it is registered under the federal Trademarks Act and no French version is registered [s31][s32].
Products made before Jun 1, 2025 can, under conditions, be sold until Jun 1, 2027 [s32].

If your products are sold to Quebec buyers, assume these rules apply to your packaging even if you are based elsewhere. The details are technical; check the Office québécois de la langue française (OQLF) or a Quebec lawyer for your case [s31].

callout.title: Simple rule
callout.text: Design one bilingual pack (English and French with equal prominence) and use it for all of Canada. It covers the federal rules and Quebec at once, and it shows buyers you are a real Canadian brand.

ul: **Brand Registry** gives you tools such as A+ Content, Brand Stores, Sponsored Brands and better protection against hijackers. You need a registered or pending trademark from an eligible office.

In Canada, trademarks are filed with the **Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO)**. Examination and registration can take a long time; check CIPO's current service standards when you file. File early, ideally before you order packaging.

Amazon's **IP Accelerator** connects you with vetted IP law firms and can give earlier Brand Registry access once a trademark is filed. Check in Brand Registry whether it is offered for CIPO filings when you apply.
If you also plan to sell in the US, consider a US trademark (USPTO) as well, since protection is country by country.

sections.title: Choosing your first product with data

blocks.h3: Criteria that work for a first Amazon.ca product

ul: Sells for about CAD 25–60, so fees leave room for profit.
Small and light: fits the envelope or standard size tier and weighs under 1 kg [s38].
Not fragile, not seasonal, no batteries or liquids, not for babies or young children.
Not gated and not regulated by special Health Canada rules.
Searched all year in both English and French.
Top listings have reviews you can realistically compete with, and visible weaknesses (bad photos, English-only, slow shipping from the US).

blocks.p: Aim for at least 30% of the price left after Amazon fees, landed product cost and ads. Using the example in the costs section, a CAD 25 item keeps about CAD 15.12 after the referral and FBA fees [s38][s4]. To keep 30% (CAD 7.50) you can spend about CAD 7.62 per unit on landed product cost, inbound shipping, storage and ads combined. If your landed cost is already CAD 5, that leaves only about CAD 2.62 for ads and storage, which is tight. This is why many beginners pick a higher price point. (Example only.)

blocks.h3: Validate demand with official Amazon tools

ol: **Product Opportunity Explorer** (Seller Central, Brand Analytics access may vary): see search volume and trends for a niche on Amazon.ca.
**Brand Analytics** (after Brand Registry): top search terms and click share.
**Revenue Calculator**: enter size, weight and price to see the exact Amazon.ca fees.
**Amazon Ads console**: suggested bids show how expensive keywords are.
Search Amazon.ca yourself in English and French and note who ranks, their reviews and their prices.
Order a few competitor products and read their 1–3 star reviews for problems you can fix.

ul: Seasonal spikes (Christmas-only or summer-only).
Fragile, heavy or oversized items.
Patented designs or famous brand look-alikes; check patents before you order.
Gated categories or Health Canada-regulated items.
US-made goods on Canada's counter-tariff list, or goods you plan to sell into the US that fall under US 50% tariffs [s20][s27].

blocks.p: Amazon's older North America Remote Fulfilment (NARF) program has been replaced by Remote Fulfilment with FBA. One 2026 fee roundup reports higher remote-fulfilment rates for Canada and Mexico [s26]. Remote orders cross the border, so buyers may face duties and slower delivery, and US-origin goods may be caught by Canadian counter-tariffs [s20]. Check enrolment, eligible products and current fees in Seller Central before you rely on it. For a serious Canadian business, stock in Canadian warehouses usually wins.

ul: Create a shipment in Send to Amazon. Label every unit with its FNSKU barcode and every box with Amazon's box label.
Follow Amazon's prep rules (poly bags, bubble wrap, suffocation warnings in English and French for bags).
If you import into Canada, you or your broker are the importer of record. Get a BN with an import-export program account, use a customs broker for your first shipments, and know your tariff code.

US goods that qualify under CUSMA can enter with lower or no duty. Commercial low-value shipments up to CAD 3,300 can use simplified courier processing [s28]. Postal shipments, and small shipments from outside the US and Mexico, keep a CAD 20 duty and tax relief threshold [s29]. Couriered CUSMA shipments are generally duty and tax free up to CAD 40 and duty free up to CAD 150 [s28]; confirm current thresholds with CBSA.
From China or India, shipments enter under normal duty rates; check the Canadian Customs Tariff for your code.
Order enough for 60–90 days of expected sales, plus time for shipping and receiving.
Send a first small batch (100–300 units) to learn real sales speed before reordering.
Watch Restock Inventory in Seller Central weekly. Running out kills your ranking; too much stock costs storage and aged fees.
Plan Q4 stock early. Peak fees start Oct 15 [s37] and warehouses get busy.

sections.title: Your first 90 days, week by week

ul: Write the title, bullets and description in clear English. Add French where Seller Central lets you (Amazon.ca shows French to French-language shoppers).
Use 7+ images: white-background main photo, close-ups, in-use photos, a size chart, and an infographic with both languages if possible.
Fill every backend field: search terms (include French terms), item type, size, material.
Price competitively but not at a loss. Check the Revenue Calculator one last time.
Once Brand Registry is active, add **A+ Content** and enrol in **Amazon Vine** to get early honest reviews from vetted reviewers.
Start Sponsored Products ads (see next section).
Use a small coupon or introductory price for the first weeks; never pay or reward anyone for a review.
Read search term reports weekly. Add winning terms to exact-match campaigns; add bad terms as negatives.
Fix listing problems the first reviews and questions reveal.
Check stock levels and reorder in time.
Build a Brand Store page.
Try Sponsored Brands if you have Brand Registry.
Plan your first deal or Prime Exclusive Discount for the next event.

head: Checkpoint
What 'good' looks like
rows: Listing live and indexed for your main keywords, first sales every day or two, first reviews from Vine, ads running with clean search-term data
Daily sales, 10+ reviews, ACoS trending down, first reorder placed, French content live
Steady organic sales, profitable or near break-even after ads, clear data on whether to add a second product or expand to the US
table.note: These are rough beginner targets, not Amazon benchmarks.

ul: **Sponsored Products**: ads for a single listing in search results and on product pages. Start here.
**Sponsored Brands**: a banner with your logo and several products. Needs Brand Registry.
**Sponsored Display**: ads shown on product pages and off Amazon to shoppers who viewed similar items.

ol: **Auto campaign**: Amazon chooses the keywords. Use it to discover search terms.
**Manual exact campaign**: 10–20 of your most relevant keywords, in English and French.
**Manual phrase/broad campaign**: a few broader terms to find more searches.
**Product targeting**: target competitor listings that are weaker than yours.

blocks.p: A starter daily budget of about CAD 20–30 across campaigns is a common planning number for a single product; use the Ads console's suggested bids to set your bids, then let campaigns run 1–2 weeks before big changes.

ul: **ACoS** (advertising cost of sale) = ad spend ÷ ad sales. If you spend CAD 30 and ads bring CAD 100 in sales, ACoS is 30%.
**TACoS** (total ACoS) = ad spend ÷ all sales (ads + organic). It shows whether ads are building organic sales.
**Break-even ACoS** = your margin before ads ÷ price. In the costs example, if a unit keeps CAD 10 before ads on a CAD 25 price, break-even ACoS is 40%.
Early on, ACoS above break-even is normal while you gather data and reviews. Aim to get under break-even by day 60–90.

blocks.p: Add search terms that spend money without sales, or are clearly irrelevant (wrong product, wrong size, 'free', other brands you don't match), as negative exact keywords. Do this every week.

ol: Download the search term report.
Move converting terms into exact campaigns.
Add wasted terms as negatives.
Lower bids on high-ACoS keywords; raise them on profitable ones.
Check that ads stop if stock is low.
Note ACoS and TACoS in a simple spreadsheet.

ul: Use **Amazon Vine** for early reviews (Brand Registry needed).
Use the **Request a Review** button in each order, or set it to run automatically through Amazon's own tools.
Inserts can ask for feedback in a neutral way, but cannot ask for positive reviews or offer anything in return.
Never pay for reviews, offer refunds or gifts for reviews, or review your own product. Amazon removes reviews and suspends accounts for this.

blocks.p: With Brand Registry, build a Brand Store, use A+ Content and look at Brand Analytics for search terms. Keep both English and French versions where you can.

ul: **Amazon.com (US)**: the biggest next step. With the unified account you can list there without a second subscription [s1][s2]. Check US tariffs first: a 10% Section 301 tariff on most Canadian goods with CUSMA exemptions, and 50% Section 338 tariffs on listed products [s24][s27]. blocks.p: Send traffic from social media, email or a blog to your listing. If you are in Brand Registry, check whether the Brand Referral Bonus program is available for Amazon.ca in your account; it can credit you part of the referral fee on sales you drive.

sections.title: Common beginner mistakes and account-health risks

ol: **Using US fee numbers.** Amazon.ca fees are in CAD and different. Use the Amazon.ca Revenue Calculator.
**Forgetting the 3.5% surcharge and peak fees.** Since Apr 17, 2026 FBA fees carry a 3.5% surcharge [s4], and peak fees run Oct 15 – Jan 14 [s37].
**English-only labels.** Missing French on product identity breaks federal rules [s33]; Quebec needs much more [s31].
**Wrong GST/HST setup.** Entering a GST/HST number means you, not Amazon, remit GST/HST [s10][s17]. Don't enter one you don't actively file.
**Ignoring tariffs.** Check both Canada's counter-tariff lists [s20] and US tariffs [s27] before importing or exporting.
**Selling a gated or unsafe product.** Children's items without testing, or products under Health Canada rules, can be removed and lead to suspensions.
**Review manipulation.** Paid reviews, review swaps, 'refund after review' deals and family reviews get accounts suspended.
**IP complaints.** Copying brand names, photos or patented designs leads to takedowns. Use your own photos and check patents.
**Inauthentic or condition complaints.** Keep supplier invoices; Amazon may ask for them. Never sell used items as new.
**Late shipments and cancellations (FBM).** Keep late shipment rate and cancellation rate low; set realistic handling times.
**Running out of stock.** You lose ranking, and it takes time and ad money to recover.
**Overstocking.** Too much stock means storage and aged-inventory fees.
**Multiple accounts.** A second account without Amazon's approval can get all your accounts suspended.
**Ignoring Account Health.** Check the Account Health page weekly and answer any notice before the deadline.
**Not keeping records.** Keep invoices, customs papers, safety tests and settlement reports for tax and Amazon audits.
Decide whether Amazon.ca is your first store or an add-on to the US.
Pick a business structure; get a Business Number from the CRA if you are Canadian [s13].
Open a bank account and get your ID and a matching statement ready.
Register a Professional seller account (CAD 29.99/month) [s1].
Complete identity verification, including any video call.
Set up two-step verification and the tax interview.
Decide whether to register for GST/HST now or later (CAD 30,000 test) [s13][s14].
Shortlist 5–10 product ideas using Product Opportunity Explorer and Amazon.ca search.
Check each idea for gating, Health Canada rules, patents and tariffs.
Run the numbers in the Revenue Calculator, including the 3.5% surcharge [s4].
Order samples from 2–3 suppliers.
File a trademark with CIPO (and USPTO if you will sell in the US).
Design bilingual packaging that meets federal rules and Bill 96 [s31][s33].
Place a small first order; arrange a customs broker if importing.
Create the listing with full English and French content and 7+ images.
Create the FBA shipment, label correctly and send stock.
Apply for Brand Registry as soon as your trademark is filed.
Add A+ Content and enrol in Vine.
Launch Sponsored Products: auto + exact + product targeting.
Run the weekly ads routine and add negatives.
Turn on Request a Review; never buy reviews.
Watch stock weekly and reorder for 60–90 days of sales.
Plan Prime Day, Black Friday and Boxing Day stock early.
Review profit at day 90, then decide: second product or Amazon.com.
Book a session with a Canadian accountant before tax season.

faq.q: How much does it cost to sell on Amazon Canada?
faq.a: The Professional plan is CAD 29.99 a month, or the Individual plan charges CAD 1.49 per unit sold. On top, you pay a referral fee per sale (15% in many categories, CAD 0.40 minimum) and, with FBA, fulfilment fees from CAD 4.46 (envelope) or CAD 5.92 (standard, first 100 g), plus a 3.5% surcharge since April 17, 2026.

faq.q: If I sign up on Amazon.ca, can I also sell on Amazon.com?
faq.a: Yes. A Professional account is a unified account that covers the US, Canadian and Mexican stores without a second subscription. If you register through the US store, the fee is USD 39.99 a month (and also covers Brazil); a Canada account used only for Canada is CAD 29.99.

faq.q: Do I need a GST number to sell on Amazon.ca?
faq.a: Not at first, for most small Canadian sellers. You must register once your taxable sales pass CAD 30,000 in a quarter or over four quarters. Until then Amazon collects and remits GST/HST on your Amazon.ca sales. You can register early to claim back the GST/HST on Amazon's fees.

faq.q: Does Amazon collect PST and QST for me?
faq.a: Amazon says it collects and remits provincial taxes in BC, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec on eligible sales shipped from within Canada. If you are registered for GST/HST or QST, check Amazon's tax page, because some of that duty shifts to you.

faq.q: I'm from India (or China). Can I sell on Amazon.ca?
faq.a: Yes, through the North America Unified Account. You'll need valid ID, a payout method and a credit card. A non-resident who isn't registered and doesn't carry on business in Canada generally doesn't need to register for GST/HST when selling through Amazon, but get advice if you store stock in Canada. Your labels still need English and French.

faq.q: Do my products really need French labels?
faq.a: Yes. Federal rules require the product identity in English and French, and Quebec's Bill 96 (Law 14) requires French on packaging, instructions and warranties. Since June 1, 2025, generic words on packaging generally need French even beside a trademark. The simplest approach is one bilingual pack for all of Canada; check the OQLF for your exact case.

faq.q: Is Amazon FBA worth it in Canada?
faq.a: For most small, light products, yes: you get Prime eligibility and Amazon handles shipping and returns. Watch fees on heavy items, plan for holiday peak fees (Oct 15 to Jan 14) and send small batches first to avoid storage costs.

faq.q: Can I ship my US FBA inventory to Canadian customers?
faq.a: Amazon's Remote Fulfilment with FBA lets US warehouse stock fill Amazon.ca orders, but buyers may pay duties, delivery is slower and US-origin goods may face Canadian counter-tariffs. It's a test tool; for steady sales, stock Canadian warehouses.

faq.q: How do US–Canada tariffs affect me as an Amazon seller?
faq.a: If you import US goods into Canada, check Canada's current counter-tariff list on canada.ca (new rates of 15–50% took effect September 8, 2026 on certain goods, and the list has been revised). If you sell Canadian goods into the US, most face a 10% US tariff unless they qualify under CUSMA, and some listed products face 50%. Rates change often, so check CBSA and US CBP before you ship.

faq.q: How long does a Canadian trademark take for Brand Registry?
faq.a: CIPO registration can take a long time, so file as early as you can and check CIPO's current processing times. Amazon's IP Accelerator can speed up Brand Registry access once a trademark is filed; check whether it covers your filing.

faq.q: What's a good ACoS for a new product?
faq.a: Work out your break-even ACoS: your profit before ads divided by the price. At launch it's normal to be above that while you collect data and reviews; aim to get below break-even by day 60 to 90.

faq.q: How do I get my first reviews without breaking the rules?
faq.a: Enrol in Amazon Vine once you have Brand Registry, and use the Request a Review button. Never pay, refund or gift anyone for a review, and never ask friends or family to review; that gets accounts suspended.

faq.q: Should I pick the Individual or Professional plan?
faq.a: Individual costs CAD 1.49 per unit sold, so it's cheaper below about 20 sales a month. Professional (CAD 29.99/month) is needed for ads, bulk tools and most brand features, so most people building a real business choose it.
